def: The first and most expensive training stage: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of text and code. Most knowledge and raw capability comes from here.

A stage between pretraining and fine-tuning that continues the same loss on curated data, often while the learning rate decays: high-quality text, long documents for context extension, or boosted code and math.
Decaying the learning rate toward zero at the end of pretraining, often on a higher-quality data mix. It produces a visible drop in loss.
The unit a language model reads and writes: a chunk of text produced by the tokenizer, often a word piece. English averages roughly four characters per token for common tokenizers.
A tokenizer training method that starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair until the vocabulary reaches a target size.
The raw, unnormalised scores a model outputs for each vocabulary item before softmax turns them into probabilities.
The function that turns logits into probabilities: exponentiate each score and divide by the sum. Temperature divides the logits first.
The average negative log probability a model assigns to the token that actually came next. The pretraining and SFT objective.
The exponential of cross-entropy loss in nats. Roughly the number of equally likely choices the model feels it faces at each token.
Total loss in bits divided by the text length in bytes. Lets you compare models with different tokenizers.
The proportions of each data source (web, code, math, books, languages, synthetic) in a training run. Tuned with small proxy models.
A near-duplicate detection method that estimates Jaccard similarity between documents' n-gram sets using the minimum of random hash functions.
A small model that scores documents for usefulness (for example educational value) so only the best slice of a web crawl is kept.
The step size of each parameter update. The most important hyperparameter in training.
Updating parameters by stepping against the gradient of the loss. With mini-batches it is stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
Accumulating a running average of past gradients so consistent directions speed up and oscillations cancel.
The standard LLM optimiser: Adam's per-parameter step scaling from running averages of the gradient and squared gradient, plus decoupled weight decay.
Ramping the learning rate up from near zero over the first steps of training, because early gradients are large and erratic.
A learning-rate schedule that decays from the peak to a minimum following half a cosine wave after warmup.
Warmup-stable-decay: hold the learning rate constant for most of training and decay only at the end, so decayed checkpoints can be branched off at any point.
The batch size beyond which larger batches give little reduction in the number of training steps. Estimated by the gradient noise scale.
Rescaling the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold (commonly 1.0) to prevent unstable updates.
A sudden jump in training loss during a large run, usually from optimisation instability. Often handled by rolling back and skipping batches.
Brain floating point: a 16-bit format with the same exponent range as fp32 but fewer mantissa bits. The standard training precision.
Training with 8-bit floating-point matrix multiplies for higher throughput and lower memory, with careful scaling to avoid overflow. Used at scale in DeepSeek-V3.
Zero Redundancy Optimizer: sharding optimiser states (stage 1), gradients (stage 2), and weights (stage 3) across data-parallel GPUs instead of replicating them.
Fully Sharded Data Parallel, PyTorch's implementation of ZeRO-style sharding of model state across GPUs.
Splitting individual weight matrices across GPUs so each computes part of every layer. Needs fast interconnect.
Placing different layers on different GPUs and streaming micro-batches through them.
Model FLOPs utilisation: useful training FLOPs per second divided by the hardware's peak. Large runs typically reach 35 to 50 percent.
Discarding intermediate activations in the forward pass and recomputing them during backward to save memory at the cost of extra compute.
An empirical power-law relationship between loss and model size, data, or compute, used to predict large runs from small ones.
Hoffmann et al. (2022): for a fixed training budget, grow parameters and tokens together, about 20 tokens per parameter.
The split of a fixed training compute budget between model size and data that minimises loss.
Training a smaller model on far more tokens than compute-optimal, accepting slightly higher loss for much cheaper inference.
An architecture where each token is routed to a few of many expert sub-networks, so total parameters can be large while per-token compute stays small.
A capability that appears to arise suddenly with scale. Often an artifact of all-or-nothing metrics; smooth metrics usually show gradual improvement.
The approximate training compute of a dense transformer: 6 FLOPs per parameter per training token (2 forward, 4 backward).
